results.title: GPU price increase in 2026: why AWS costs keep rising | AI Compute Marketplace | Compare GPU Cloud & Data Centers | ComputeStacker Insights
highlights:
Industry-wide, GPU prices are rising in 2026. The demand for AI is growing faster than the supply of chips to run it. AWS is an excellent example of a provider that has increased its prices twice so far this year, and there’s a third increase planned according to its official pricing page.

## Key takeaways

- GPU prices are increasing across the industry in 2026 as AI demand outpaces chip supply.
- AWS has increased EC2 Capacity Block GPU pricing twice in 2026: once in January by around 15% and again in July by around 20%.
- According to AWS’s own pricing page, there is another price hike due in October 2026.
- The price hikes only apply to reserved Capacity Block pricing, not on-demand or Savings Plans.
- There are legitimate alternatives to AWS reserved capacity for buyers to consider.

...

There are four reasons for increasing prices at almost every provider, not only in AWS.

The demand for AI training and inference outpaces the supply of accelerators. Each new release of models increases the demand on computations compared to the previous generation of models.

Chip manufacturing has not fulfilled it yet. It results in a growing mismatch between supply and demand instead of narrowing it.

...

We analyzed pricing from 150+ GPU cloud providers to find the exact threshold where an AI startup's OpenAI API bill eclipses the cost of a dedicated H100 cluster.

The industry faces a limited supply of high-end GPUs. The GPU capacity crunch has affected rental costs in the industry already this year.

It looks like there are no signs of this situation being reversed soon. Big AI labs make big computation orders, taking resources out of general circulation and preventing smaller players from accessing them.

The companies have introduced more expensive next-generation GPUs. Blackwell-class chips require more energy, better cooling systems, and better networking capabilities.

These extra expenses transfer directly into the cost of renting. Providers cannot absorb higher costs and pass nothing through.

Higher costs of data centre infrastructure exacerbate the problem. Energy, cooling, and high-speed networking have become more expensive. It is not at the expense of providers’ margins alone.

## Why AWS GPU prices are especially visible right now

AWS provides the clearest, easiest-to-track example of this general trend, thanks to the specificity and public dating of these changes.

First, AWS increased EC2 Capacity Block prices by roughly 15% on January 4, 2026. According to DataCenterDynamics, this was the first price increase for this product ever.

The p5e.48xlarge GPU instance has increased its hourly price in almost all regions from $34.61 to $39.80. With p5en.48xlarge, the price jumped from $36.18 to $41.61. Even US West got a rise from $43.26 to $49.75.

The second price increase occurred on July 1. They estimated the increase to be around 20% and applied it to the newest generations of the company’s products, not just to the existing H100-based fleet.

Here is how AWS’s own live pricing page shows prices today for its GPU instance families:

| Instance type | Chip | Rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | Blackwell Ultra | $14.04/accelerator-hr |
| P6-B200 | Blackwell | $12.355/accelerator-hr |
| P5en | H200 | $6.865/hr (US) |
| P5e | H200 | $5.97/hr |
| P5 | H100 | $5.191/hr (US) |
| P4de | A100 | $2.214/hr (US) |

There is even more. As AWS states on its pricing page, the next price change will happen in October 2026. Articles covering the two price increases of 2026 never mention this aspect.

AWS has said not much about the reasons behind price changes. They were just attributed to “periodic pricing updates tied to supply and demand”.

...

## How AWS GPU pricing actually works

Not all AWS GPU users bore these price increases equally. The price increase was applicable only to the Capacity Block category, which is a reservation product of AWS offering guaranteed GPU capacity within a certain period.

Pricing models like the price increase have not affected on-demand and Savings Plans, and knowing that will help you decide which pricing model you should choose yourself.

The reason behind the existence of Capacity Block is that there is some extra value in the guaranteed access to scarce GPU capacity. You pay not only for the compute but for the guaranteed access to it as well, which is why AWS can raise the prices in this category.

Reservation periods are available for one day to several months, depending on the particular instance types and their availability. Shorter reservations are normally more expensive compared to longer reservations.

Apart from the reservation cost, AWS charges separately for operating system installation, except for Linux, which is free.

...

Predictability has become trickier in reserved capacity pricing models. While the rate was steady for years, rates have already increased twice within a single year. AWS plans to introduce a third increase in October.

It could still make sense to secure a reservation under certain circumstances.

...

When you plan to renew or extend any existing AWS Capacity Block commitment, compare the present rate with the one you’ve been paying. The commitment that was made prior to January or July could be outdated at the moment.

Of course, consider the total cost and the initial per-hour cost. Sometimes, a higher per-hour cost with a smaller commitment may be better than a lower per-hour cost with a long commitment. Considering how pricing has changed over the past year, this matters immensely.

...

AWS increased the cost of EC2 Capacity Block two times. By 15% in January and by 20% in July. It is clear from AWS’s own page that there is going to be a third update in October 2026.

...

No, AWS restricted both 2026 increases to Capacity Blocks, the reservation offering of AWS. The changes did not affect on-demand prices and savings, although this might change with the upcoming October announcement.

results.title: The same GPU, at very different prices · infratoapp
highlights:
## The finding

30 GPU models are rented on-demand by 3 or more of the providers listed here. On every one of them, the providers disagree about the price — and on most, they disagree by more than a rounding error.

The median gap between the cheapest and dearest seller of an identical card is 3.8×. The widest is the V100-16GB: $0.24 per GPU-hour at Verda (DataCrunch) against $2.85 at Runcrate, a gap of 11.8×. An H100 SXM 80GB — the card most of this market is actually built on — runs from $2.16 to $6.16 across 13 sellers, a gap of 2.8×.

These are headline on-demand rates, before any commitment discount, for the same part. Not a similar part, not a different memory configuration, and not one region against another.

...

Four constraints decide whether a number like this means anything, and each one removes rows we would rather have kept.

On-demand only. A spot rate is a different product and a committed rate is a different contract; putting them in one range would compare things nobody chooses between.

One rate per seller per card, their cheapest. A provider listing an H100 at four instance sizes is one seller with one headline rate. Counting each instance size separately would let a single price list manufacture a spread on its own.

Headline rates rather than regional ones. Comparing Virginia against Frankfurt and calling the difference a market would be a mistake about geography wearing the costume of a finding.

A minimum of 3 sellers. A couple of providers disagreeing is an anecdote. This bar is what reduces the set to the 30 cards compared, and it is the constraint we would relax last.

...

Across the 30 cards compared, the lowest rate tends to sit with marketplaces and community clouds rather than managed providers. The widest gap, on the V100-16GB, is Verda (DataCrunch) against Runcrate.

That is a fact about price and nothing else. It says nothing about availability when you need a whole cluster at once, about what happens when an instance is reclaimed, about support, or about whether the network between your nodes is any good. Those differences are most of why the dearer providers exist, and none of them are visible in a per-hour rate.

So this is not a buying recommendation, and there is no "best value" column anywhere on this site. The number tells you what to ask about, not what to choose.

results.title: The same H100 rents for $1.79 an hour from one provider and $10.00 from another. | Mercatus AI | The Open Intelligence Exchange
highlights:
# The same H100 rents for $1.79 an hour from one provider and $10.00 from another. | Mercatus AI | The Open Intelligence Exchange · LinkedIn · 2026-09-16T00:00:00+00:00

**Mercatus AI | The Open Intelligence Exchange**.

---

The same H100 rents for $1.79 an hour from one provider and $10.00 from another.

Not a different GPU. Not a different region. Same 80GB SXM5 card, on-demand, this week.

We track 27 providers on the Mercatus GPU Index. Here is where the market sits as of September 13:

H100: $3.84/hr average, range $1.79 to $12.52
H200: $4.43/hr average, range $2.25 to $11.71
B200: $6.39/hr average, range $3.74 to $16.14

On an 8-GPU H100 node running around the clock, that spread is $11,400 a month at the cheapest provider and $58,400 at the most expensive. A $47,000 gap on identical hardware.

The gap between an average H100 node and an average B200 node is $15,000.

A posted rate card tells you what one seller wants, not what the market price is. Same lesson as tokens.

results.title: The GPU capacity crunch didn't hit every pricing tier the same way this year. | Compute Stacker
highlights:
The GPU capacity crunch didn't hit every pricing tier the same way this year.
Reserved H100 pricing is up ~40% since October, climbing from $1.70 to $2.35 an hour. Spot pricing on the same chip fell over the same stretch. Same chip, same period, moving in opposite directions.
That's not a typo. It's what happens when the real bottleneck moves from chip fabrication to memory supply, HBM and CoWoS packaging capacity specifically, not GPU dies.
Full breakdown in the video. If you want to see where that gap actually sits today across providers, that's what we track at ComputeStacker.

results.title: GPU prices fell 75% this year. GPU prices rose 40% this year. | Fergus McKenzie-Wilson
highlights:
GPU prices fell 75% this year. GPU prices rose 40% this year.
Both are true, and the gap between them is what people get wrong about AI infrastructure.

Everyone says that the people building AI compute are the new kingmakers.
I spoke with my friend Oscar Gompels, who's handing out the crowns himself and mapped 251 companies doing it. Here's what I learnt:

Take the pricing first. On-demand H100 rates fell about 75% from the 2023 peak. One-year reserved contracts rose 40% between October 2025 and March 2026. Spot capacity deflates as each generation matures. Contracted capacity inflates while the shortage holds. Quote one number and you have described half a market.

Now the kingmaker question. The companies renting you GPUs carry obsolescence risk, utilisation risk and refinancing risk at the same time. Post-depreciation margins across the category run 14 to 16%. Applied Digital earns over 25% leasing them the building. Broadcom booked $16.7bn of AI semiconductor revenue in one quarter, up 221%. VAST Data sells the storage layer, runs cash positive, and raised at $30bn. Almost everyone supplying the neoclouds has a better business than the neoclouds.

CoreWeave holds the only Platinum reliability rating in the sector, two ratings running, scored on security, health checks, networking and orchestration rather than price.
It lists H100 capacity near $6.16 an hour against rivals at $3.85 and sells out anyway, because a failed run on ten thousand GPUs costs more than the rate card difference.
It re-leased three year old H100s at 95% of original pricing and has A100s contracted through 2029. That is the strongest published evidence against the idea that a GPU is worthless after three years, and it came from an operator willing to disclose it.
Its backlog reached $104bn, and the share running beyond four years doubled in a year.
